title: Josiah & the Last Decades of Judah
subtitle: Reform, Megiddo, Carchemish, and the geopolitical collapse that precedes Babylonian domination.

chapters.title: Josiah in Jerusalem
chapters.description: Begin in Jerusalem, where Kings locates Josiah’s reform program. Archaeology supplies the city context, not a labeled “room of Josiah.”

chapters.title: Late Iron Age textual world
chapters.description: Silver amulets from nearby Ketef Hinnom preserve wording related to the priestly blessing. They illuminate the era without identifying a biblical owner.

chapters.title: Megiddo, 609 BCE
chapters.description: Josiah dies in the Megiddo campaign context as Necho II moves north. Kings and Chronicles differ in detail, so the atlas does not overstate motives.

chapters.title: Carchemish, 605 BCE
chapters.description: Four years later Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish, transforming the strategic world in which Judah operates.

title: From Assyria’s Shadow to Babylon — The Late Prophets
subtitle: Manasseh, Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Nineveh’s fall, Jerusalem’s catastrophe, Obadiah, and the transition to exile.

chapters.title: Manasseh under Assyria
chapters.eyebrow: Seventh century BCE · biblical + Assyrian evidence
chapters.description: Assyrian royal lists independently name Manasseh king of Judah, placing Jerusalem inside the Neo-Assyrian imperial system without validating every later narrative detail.

chapters.title: Zephaniah’s wide horizon
chapters.description: The oracles move from Jerusalem to Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Nineveh. The map treats this as a literary-geographic horizon, not a travel itinerary.

chapters.title: Nineveh falls
chapters.description: Babylonian chronicle evidence records the coalition capture of Nineveh. This anchors the historical transition without fixing the composition date of Nahum.

chapters.title: The Chaldeans rise
chapters.eyebrow: Late seventh / early sixth century BCE
chapters.description: Habakkuk’s Chaldeans belong to the Babylonian ascendance after Assyria’s collapse, but the book does not give a single externally fixed date.

chapters.title: Jerusalem mourned
chapters.description: Lamentations is tied to destroyed Jerusalem as poetry and theology; the atlas does not turn the poems into a street-by-street archaeological report.

chapters.title: Edom and Jerusalem
chapters.description: Obadiah’s Edom/Jerusalem setting is clear, but the exact historical moment is debated. Teman remains unpinned.

title: Jeremiah — From Anathoth to the Fall of Jerusalem
subtitle: A prophetic geography of Anathoth, Jerusalem, Hinnom, siege, Mizpah, and Egypt.

chapters.title: Anathoth
chapters.description: Jeremiah is introduced as a priest from Anathoth. The village identification is probable; his specific household is not recoverable.

chapters.title: Hinnom and Topheth
chapters.description: The Hinnom valley can be mapped, but Topheth itself is left without a fake coordinate.

chapters.title: The scroll under Jehoiakim
chapters.description: The royal-scroll episode belongs to Jerusalem, but no manuscript or chamber is claimed archaeologically.

chapters.title: The city falls
chapters.description: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. The atlas keeps the common 587/586 BCE one-year chronological variation visible.

chapters.title: Mizpah after Jerusalem
chapters.description: Gedaliah’s administration shifts the narrative focus to Mizpah after the city’s fall.

chapters.title: Refugees reach Tahpanhes
chapters.description: After Gedaliah’s assassination, survivors travel to Egypt. Tahpanhes is probably Tell Defenneh; Migdol remains unpinned.

title: Jerusalem → Babylon — Conquest and Exile
subtitle: 597 BCE, 587/586 BCE, royal deportation, Babylonian evidence, and Judean life in exile.

chapters.title: Jerusalem captured
chapters.description: Jehoiachin’s deportation is one of the atlas’s strongest independently dated intersections between biblical narrative and Babylonian chronicle evidence.

chapters.title: Babylon
chapters.description: Babylon is no generic symbol here: it is an excavated city and administrative capital with an enormous cuneiform record.

chapters.title: Yaukin in ration tablets
chapters.description: Babylonian tablets name Yaukin, king of Judah, and members of his household—independent evidence for the exiled Judean court.

chapters.title: Judeans in Babylonia
chapters.description: Later documents show Judean families farming, contracting, and living within Babylonian society. Al-Yahudu itself remains unpinned.

title: Ezekiel by the Kebar
subtitle: Exile geography, prophetic chronology, Jerusalem visions, and the difference between canals and visions.

chapters.title: By the Kebar
chapters.eyebrow: Babylonian canal context · approximate map area
chapters.description: Ezekiel locates himself among exiles by the Kebar. The atlas deliberately does not confuse it with the northern Khabur River.

chapters.title: Tel-abib
chapters.description: Ezekiel’s settlement cannot be securely located, so the story keeps it textual rather than inventing coordinates.

chapters.title: Jerusalem in vision
chapters.description: Ezekiel 8–11 describes visionary transport. The app distinguishes that from an animated terrestrial journey.

chapters.title: Visionary temple
chapters.description: The final temple vision is not drawn as an excavated Persian or Iron Age building footprint.

title: Daniel — Babylon, Susa, and Imperial Visions
subtitle: Map the historical places while keeping court tales, visionary geography, and debated rulers epistemically distinct.

chapters.title: Babylonian court setting
chapters.description: Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon are historical. Daniel 1’s individual court biography is presented as the book’s literary/biblical setting rather than external archival fact.

chapters.title: Plain of Dura
chapters.description: Daniel 3 gives a Babylonian provincial setting, but no Dura candidate is secure enough for a pin.

chapters.title: 539 BCE
chapters.description: The fall of Babylon is independently dated. Belshazzar is historical; “Darius the Mede” remains historically unresolved.

chapters.title: Susa and the Ulai
chapters.description: Daniel 8 names Susa and the Ulai. Susa is secure; the canal is shown only approximately.

chapters.title: The Tigris
chapters.description: Daniel 10 names the Tigris but not a precise modern location along it.

title: Cyrus, Babylon, and the Return
subtitle: 539 BCE conquest, Persian restoration ideology, Ezra’s decree tradition, and return to Jerusalem.

chapters.title: Persian royal heartland
chapters.description: Pasargadae anchors Cyrus’s Iranian royal world; it is context, not a biblical event site.

chapters.title: Babylon falls
chapters.description: Persian forces take Babylon, ending Neo-Babylonian rule.

chapters.title: What the Cyrus Cylinder actually says
chapters.description: The cylinder describes restoration in Babylonian royal language but does not name Jerusalem, Judah, Judeans, or the Jerusalem temple.

chapters.title: Ezra’s decree tradition
chapters.description: Ezra credits Cyrus with authorizing temple restoration. The app connects this to Persian policy context without claiming the cylinder is the Jerusalem decree.

title: Zerubbabel, Haggai & Zechariah — Rebuilding the Temple
subtitle: Early Yehud, Darius I, prophetic dates, and the Second Temple without a fabricated floor plan.

chapters.title: Yehud under Persia
chapters.description: Persian-period Judah is shown as Yehud, with borders intentionally approximate.

chapters.title: Haggai’s dated challenge
chapters.description: Haggai addresses Zerubbabel and Joshua/Jeshua during Darius I’s reign.

chapters.title: Zechariah’s visions
chapters.description: Zechariah’s early visions belong to the same Persian setting while remaining prophetic/visionary literature.

chapters.title: Temple completed
chapters.description: Ezra dates completion to Darius year 6. The atlas maps the Temple Mount but refuses to draw an invented Persian-period architectural plan.

title: Esther at Susa
subtitle: Achaemenid palace geography, Ahasuerus/Xerxes, and the difference between a historical court setting and independently verified narrative.

chapters.title: The citadel of Susa
chapters.description: Susa’s Achaemenid palace complex is real and excavated. The story does not label a particular room as Esther’s banquet space.

chapters.title: From India to Cush
chapters.eyebrow: Literary imperial scope · historical Achaemenid world
chapters.description: Esther depicts a vast empire. The timeline shows a generalized Persian imperial context rather than interpreting the phrase as a surveyed map polygon.

chapters.title: Ahasuerus and Xerxes
chapters.eyebrow: Common identification · not every episode externally attested
chapters.description: Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I on linguistic/historical grounds; the individual plot is not documented in surviving royal archives.

chapters.title: Purim narrative
chapters.description: The atlas presents Esther’s diaspora court geography without converting absence or presence of external evidence into a verdict on faith claims.

title: Ezra — Torah and the Road to Jerusalem
subtitle: Babylonian diaspora, unlocated Ahava/Casiphia, debated chronology, and Jerusalem reform.

chapters.title: From Babylonia
chapters.description: Ezra emerges from the Persian-period Babylonian diaspora world, where Judean communities are independently attested.

chapters.title: Ahava and Casiphia
chapters.description: Both are kept in the database and search, but neither receives a fake map coordinate.

chapters.title: Toward Jerusalem
chapters.description: The route animation connects the broad endpoints while explicitly skipping invented coordinates for Ahava and Casiphia.

chapters.title: When did Ezra arrive?
chapters.description: 458 BCE under Artaxerxes I is traditional, but later chronologies have been proposed. The data model keeps that uncertainty visible.

chapters.title: Torah reading in Jerusalem
chapters.description: The public reading belongs to Jerusalem; the exact Water Gate square is not pinned.

title: Nehemiah — Susa to Jerusalem
subtitle: A Persian imperial journey, Yehud governorship, wall reconstruction, and independently documented fifth-century context.

chapters.title: Susa
chapters.description: Nehemiah 1 begins at the Susa citadel. The physical city is secure; his exact chamber is not.

chapters.title: Beyond the River
chapters.description: Royal letters are addressed to governors west of the Euphrates. The province is rendered broadly rather than as a modern border.

chapters.title: Inspecting Jerusalem
chapters.description: Nehemiah surveys ruined walls, but the exact fifth-century circuit and every gate identification remain debated.

chapters.title: Samaria, Ammon, Arabia
chapters.description: Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem place Yehud inside a wider western Persian political landscape.

chapters.title: A wider Persian Jewish world
chapters.description: Later Elephantine correspondence independently reveals Judean/Jewish institutions and links to Jerusalem/Samaria. It is context, not a continuation of Nehemiah’s plot.
